all_of: the bundle is a Linux authentication artifact pair: a text auth.log (or secure) and a binary wtmp
the question set asks who authenticated, from where, when, and what the session then did
at least one source address produced failed password attempts AND a later acceptance
any_of: a UTC timestamp is requested, which only wtmp can answer
a session number is requested, which only the systemd-logind record carries
an account or group was created during the window

chain.action: classify the bundle with tools/forensics/artifact_inventory.py; confirm the pair is a text auth.log plus a binary wtmp and that no absent parser is needed
chain.why: this is the one DFIR family on this box that needs no install, so it is the cheapest to work and the first worth trying

chain.action: run tools/forensics/linux_auth.py --authlog <log> --summary and read succeeded_after_failures per address, not the failure count
chain.why: the address with the most failures is the loudest scanner; the one that answers the question is the address whose failures are FOLLOWED by an acceptance

chain.action: filter --event accepted to name the account, keeping the raw line as the evidence excerpt
chain.why: the acceptance is what proves entry; a failure count is evidence about scanning only

chain.action: filter the wtmp records with --ut-type USER_PROCESS plus --ip <the address from step 2> and --user <the account from step 3>
chain.why: the bundle holds interactive sessions from a legitimate administrator at a different address across several weeks, so an unfiltered pick of the latest login selects a legitimate session. The pivot narrows 29 records to 1

chain.action: read time_utc from that single wtmp record, never a parsed auth.log time
chain.why: auth.log carries no year and no timezone offset at all; wtmp carries tv_sec, a real UTC epoch. This is the only artifact in the pair that can answer a UTC question

chain.action: filter --event logind-session and select the New session record belonging to that account and time
chain.why: three numbers in this log read like a session id - the sshd PID, the sshd `id N`, and logind New session N - and only the logind one is the session number asked for

chain.action: filter --event useradd and --event group-member for the account created and the group it was added to
chain.why: the new-user line names the account; the usermod line names the privilege. They are two different answers from two different records

chain.action: filter --event sudo and quote the COMMAND= value verbatim
chain.why: a sudo line records the command as REQUESTED; it is not proof the command succeeded, so the claim must stay at what was run

first_confirming_probe.expected: address_ranking holds at least one entry with succeeded_after_failures true, carrying both a failure count and first_accepted_line as a verbatim auth.log line
first_confirming_probe.falsifier: every address with failed attempts has accepted 0, so no brute force succeeded on this host and the authentication-trace class is closed for this bundle

blast_radius: none: every artifact is supplied and read-only, there is no target to mutate and no live host involved. The only real risk in this category is the opposite one - answering a UTC question from auth.log, whose times carry no year and no timezone, which produces a confidently wrong answer rather than any damage.

verification.evidence: Each answer was read from a supplied artifact and recorded through tools/hooks.py pre-flag --source artifact, with the record excerpt pasted from tools/forensics/linux_auth.py output rather than retyped; the tool builds each record's raw line from the unpacked bytes so the excerpt and the artifact cannot disagree. tools/decide.py returned record_solve for Brutus-q3. Answer VALUES are deliberately not recorded in this card or in solved/htb-brutus.md: a Sherlock answer is a graded secret exactly as a flag is, and both files are committed. Measured coverage: 385 auth.log lines parsed with 0 unparsed, 29 wtmp records, and 7 of the 8 questions answerable directly from the two artifacts.

reuse_when: the bundle is a Linux authentication pair - auth.log or secure, plus wtmp or btmp - rather than Windows event logs
a question asks which source address brute-forced the host and which account it reached
a question asks for a UTC login time and the only candidates are a host-local syslog and a binary utmp
a question asks for an SSH session NUMBER
a question asks what account was added for persistence, or what was run through sudo
an attack-defense estate must be checked for who logged in and what they left behind, where these are the only authentication artifacts a Linux host produces
known_traps: auth.log carries NO YEAR and NO TIMEZONE OFFSET; a tool that assumes the current year is wrong by whole years and looks right, so a UTC timestamp must come from wtmp, whose tv_sec is a real UTC epoch
ranking source addresses by failure count names the loudest scanner, not the one that got in; order on failures FOLLOWED by an acceptance

three numbers in one auth.log all read like a session id - the sshd PID in brackets, `Starting session: shell on pts/N ... id 0`, and systemd-logind `New session N` - and only the last is the session number a question means

the wtmp set contains legitimate administrator sessions from a different address spanning weeks, so the attacker record must be selected by the address recovered from the brute-force question; without that pivot the latest interactive login is a legitimate one
there are several logind New session records, so the one for the compromised account still has to be chosen by user and time rather than taken as the only match
btmp holds FAILED logins while wtmp holds successful ones; reporting a btmp record as a login is a wrong answer, so always record which file a record came from
a trailing partial record in wtmp means the file is truncated or still being written, which is itself a finding - a parser that silently drops the tail hides it
a sudo COMMAND= line records what was requested, not that it succeeded
a rotated log is several files (auth.log.1, auth.log.2.gz) and the earliest event is often in one nobody opened; state which files were actually read
.bash_history has no timestamps unless HISTTIMEFORMAT was set and is written on shell exit, so a still-open session may be absent entirely

one question in this Sherlock asks for a MITRE ATT&CK sub-technique id, which appears in NO artifact: it is published knowledge, so recording it through pre-flag --source artifact would claim an artifact read that never happened
